currentContext.strengths: Extensive distribution ecosystem with 9,900+ dealers and 24,500+ sub-dealers|Application-specific product architecture under the Right Product for the Right Application (RPRA) approach, spanning blended cement, OPC and construction chemicals|Captive and green power integration - 53.15 MW WHRS, 165.79 MW wind farms and 193 MW thermal power - reducing dependence on purchased power|Credit ratings of AA+ Stable (ICRA/CRISIL, long-term borrowings) and A1+ (short-term borrowings)|Dedicated concrete testing laboratories across facilities and a MACE division that educates users on scientific application of products|Regionally diversified integrated network across South and East India built from a single plant in Tamil Nadu, giving market proximity|Adjacent construction chemicals platform (Hard Worker) extending the Company's role across the construction ecosystem, with 5.86 lakh tons sold in the year against 3.26 lakh tons in the previous year
currentContext.strategies: Ramp up operations in 2026-27 by converting commissioned and to-be-commissioned capacity into productive volumes without compromising realisation quality|Deepen channel presence by strengthening the next generation of dealer relationships in cement while scaling the Hard Worker construction chemicals distribution network across India|Sustain financial momentum through margin recovery, cost management and further reduction of net debt as operating cash flows strengthen|Prioritise margin recovery over volume-led growth in a soft pricing environment|Monetise non-core assets and deploy the proceeds to reduce net debt while continuing to invest in capacity and efficiency|Improve blending optimisation and product chemistry through R&D to raise the clinker conversion ratio and increase the share of composite cement in the production mix|Energy optimisation - meet a growing share of energy needs from green power through wholly owned wind and WHRS assets, avoiding group captive or third-party ownership structures|Manage blended fuel cost through calibrated switching between pet coke and coal based on calorific efficiency and relative economics|Disciplined capital allocation focused on debottlenecking and optimal utilisation of existing assets as an economical route to capacity addition|Strengthen premium product share in Southern markets and sharpen go-to-market on product placement, customer engagement and realisations|Circular economy adoption - advancing fossil fuel substitution through alternative fuels and waste-derived energy sources, reducing the clinker-to-cement ratio by augmenting the proportion of supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), and implementing a zero waste to landfill strategy with material reuse across operations|Establishing a comprehensive GHG inventory covering Scope 1 (direct fuel combustion, ozone-depleting substances), Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and Scope 3 (value chain) emissions, with targeted reduction through WHRS deployment, renewable energy scaling, energy efficiency and transition to lower-carbon fuels|Transitioning away from coal-intensive power generation to align with net-zero commitments, and expanding renewable energy infrastructure (wind energy, WHRS) targeting a substantial renewable energy contribution aligned to a decarbonisation roadmap|Water stewardship - zero effluent discharge and comprehensive water recycling across operations, rainwater harvesting infrastructure, targeted mitigation for borewell groundwater extraction in stressed regions, and quantitative and qualitative monitoring of water table levels across mining operations|Occupational safety - maintaining ISO 45001 certification across operational sites, safety training from the first day of employment for permanent and contract workers, continuous monthly rotational training, the Golden Helmet Initiative, and pursuing zero-accident targets across facilities|Habitat and ecological restoration - integrating biodiversity management throughout mining lifecycles with systematic progressive mine closure planning, green cover through strategic afforestation including Miyawaki plantation methods, transforming mined-out areas into eco-parks, and supporting conservation of critically endangered Tropical Dry Evergreen Forests; progressive mine closure practices earned consecutive 5-star Ministry of Mines ratings|Logistics decarbonisation - gradually shifting from road to rail transport for key materials while exploring electric vehicle adoption, with GPS tracking and real-time vehicle monitoring and mandated driver safety measures|Rolling out a comprehensive supply chain policy covering environmental stewardship, equitable labour practices, human rights, diversity, inclusion and ethical conduct, with ESG assessments of value chain partners, vendor training and digital supply chain visibility|Human rights - embedding human rights clauses in vendor agreements covering labour principles, prohibition of child and forced labour, freedom of association, collective bargaining, non-discrimination, workplace safety and social security, with compliance assessments across all plants and offices and grievance mechanisms with defined resolution timelines|Workforce development and diversity - structured technical, leadership and digital training, campus recruitment, mentorship and succession planning, alongside diversity, equal opportunity and non-discriminatory practices with human rights training and grievance redressal|Community engagement - engaging local communities during all project expansions and greenfield projects, nodal officers at all facilities for community grievances, dedicated CSR teams and budgets at each location, quality educational institutions with accessible fees for rural children and skill development programmes for local youth
currentContext.expansion: Expansion in 2025-26 centred on Kolimigundla, debottlenecking of existing units, a new limestone block in Karnataka and the construction chemicals footprint. At Kolimigundla the railway siding was commissioned in July 2025 as previously indicated, and Line II - comprising 3.15 MTPA of clinkerisation, 1.50 MTPA of cement grinding and a 15.00 MW Waste Heat Recovery System - progressed with the cement mill commissioned in July 2025 and the rest of the project to be commissioned in 2026-27; clinker for Line II grinding will be met from Line I clinkerisation. The Company has also identified opportunities to raise Kolimigundla cement grinding capacity from 1.50 MTPA to 3.00 MTPA, expected to be completed by March 2027, and management states Line II with 3.15 MTPA of clinker and 3 MTPA of cement is expected to be commissioned in March 2027. A Quartzite mineral has been included in the existing Andhra Pradesh mining lease, intended for manufactured sand and pozzolanic additives, with statutory approvals (mining plan, environmental clearance, consent to establish and operate) being pursued. De-bottlenecking continues as an economical route to capacity addition: at Ariyalur the Line I and Line II grinding systems have been de-bottlenecked, raising combined cement grinding capacity from 3.50 MTPA to 5.50 MTPA; at Ramasamy Raja Nagar ongoing work would raise clinkerisation from 2.14 MTPA to 2.76 MTPA and cement grinding from 3.00 MTPA to 4.00 MTPA; at Jayanthipuram clinker capacity would rise from 4.61 MTPA to 5.62 MTPA and cement capacity from 3.65 MTPA to 4.35 MTPA. For the proposed cement plant at Bommanahalli (Kalaburagi District, Karnataka) the Company became the Successful Bidder for the limestone block and had, as on 31st March 2026, acquired 966.725 acres of limestone bearing lands and 83.80 acres of factory land at a cost of Rs. 261.25 crores, with further acquisitions in progress; MoEF & CC has issued environmental clearance for mining of 4 MTPA of limestone, the Consent to Establish application is at final stages with KSPCB, and the time extension for execution of the mining lease deed is valid up to 10th May 2027, with Rs. 5.24 crores incurred on preliminary mining-related expenditure. In construction chemicals, the Company operates plants at Sriperumbudur, Salem, Ramasamy Raja Nagar and Jayanthipuram and commissioned its fifth plant at Haridaspur, Jajpur District, Odisha during the year. On green power, WHRS capacity was expanded from 45.15 MW to 53.15 MW. The Company states it incurred Rs. 996.65 crores towards capital expenditure during the year under review. Environmental impact assessments during the year covered the East Band Limestone Mine, Amalgamated Periyanagalur Limestone Mine, Ottakovil Limekankar Quarry Lease-2, Expansion of Kalavatla Line-II, Bommanalli Limestone Mine Block, Expansion of Ramasamy Raja Nagar Cement Plant, Maravarperungudi Lime Kankar Quarry Lease-III and Expansion of Jayanthipuram cement plant.

risks.risk: Greenhouse gas emissions and climate change
risks.note: Cement production is carbon-intensive, with significant CO2 emissions from limestone calcination and fossil fuel combustion. The Company states escalating emissions would impact business continuity, attract regulatory scrutiny, increase compliance obligations and expose it to transition and physical climate risks affecting operational stability.

risks.risk: Energy management and dependence on coal-based captive power
risks.note: Flagged as both risk and opportunity: dependence on coal-based captive power poses transition risks in a decarbonising economy with evolving regulatory frameworks, mitigated by transitioning away from coal-intensive generation and expanding wind and WHRS investment.

Operations span water-stressed and water-surplus regions requiring location-specific management. Water scarcity has demonstrated operational and community vulnerability affecting production continuity, and competing demands threaten operational stability and the social licence to operate.

Capital-intensive cement manufacturing carries inherent operational hazards; inadequate safety management may cause injuries, fatalities, legal liabilities, operational disruption, reputational damage and workforce morale erosion affecting productivity.

Brand equity and operational continuity are linked to supply chain resilience. Disruptions or reputational concerns from value chain partners may adversely affect material availability, production schedules and stakeholder confidence.

risks.risk: Sustainable supply chain and logistics - road transport dependence
risks.note: Current reliance on road transport for key materials generates significant Scope 3 emissions affecting the carbon footprint, and enhanced monitoring of transportation vehicles is required for oversight of routes, emissions, driver behaviour and safety compliance.

risks.risk: Human rights across operations and the value chain
risks.note: Operations and value chain engage large workforce populations - permanent employees, contract workers, transport partners and multi-tier suppliers - and systematic monitoring of transport partners and deeper-tier suppliers beyond contractual clauses requires enhanced due diligence.

Digital infrastructure underpins operational continuity, with enterprise systems directly controlling critical functions such as logistics dispatch and production management. Ransomware is identified as the primary threat, with potential system shutdowns, operational disruption, compromised intellectual property and data breach affecting stakeholder trust.

risks.risk: Community relations and social licence to operate
risks.note: Community relations determine the social licence to operate and are fundamental to environmental clearances, mining licences, land access and operational continuity.

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: The Company manufactures cement (blended cement and Ordinary Portland Cement) and, through its Hard Worker brand, a range of construction chemicals covering waterproofing, tiling, flooring, masonry, block fixing, repair, grouting and wall-finishing applications. It also runs a Wind Farm division and captive thermal and waste-heat power at its cement plants. Products are sold to residential, commercial, industrial, infrastructure, marine and precast construction demand through a dealer and sub-dealer network, serving both commercial (B2B) and private (B2C) customers including trade partners, non-trade clients and government entities.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Cement demand remained structurally supported but growth was uneven - early and excess monsoons in the South compressed first-half volumes and completion of infrastructure projects in the east moderated B2B offtake
- Pricing remained under pressure for much of the year as industry capacity additions continued to outpace demand growth
- Input costs rose - a mineral-bearing land tax on limestone in Tamil Nadu from April 2025 added approximately Rs. 150 crores to input costs for the year
- Structural demand drivers remain in place: infrastructure investment, the government's housing programme and urban development in Tier-II and Tier-III cities under the City Economic Regions initiative
- India's real GDP for 2026-27 is projected at 6.8-7.2%, though domestic demand may moderate amid rising input costs
- Public capital expenditure budgeted at Rs. 12.22 lakh crores for 2026-27 at 4.4% of GDP, with continued outlays on Bharatmala, Sagarmala, Smart Cities, UDAN, high-speed rail and dedicated freight corridors that improve freight efficiency for bulk commodities such as cement
- Affordable housing support through PMAY-Urban 2.0, PMAY-Gramin and the next phase of SWAMIH last-mile funding for stalled housing projects
- GST on cement reduced from 28% to 18% effective 22nd September 2025, expected to improve cost efficiency across the value chain and drive demand in infrastructure and housing
- India's per capita cement consumption of approximately 290 kg versus a global average of 540 kg indicates strong headroom
- Cement industry volume growth of approximately 6-7% expected in 2025-26, with an estimated 160-170 million metric tonnes of capacity to be commissioned by 2027-28
- Industry trends: transition towards low-carbon cement via alternative fuels and blended cement, digitalisation and process innovation, and demand diversification into Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets
- Risk to the outlook from Middle East geopolitical tension and Strait of Hormuz disruption raising energy, freight and insurance costs and pressuring input costs and margins

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Expansion in 2025-26 centred on Kolimigundla, debottlenecking of existing units, a new limestone block in Karnataka and the construction chemicals footprint. At Kolimigundla the railway siding was commissioned in July 2025 as previously indicated, and Line II - comprising 3.15 MTPA of clinkerisation, 1.50 MTPA of cement grinding and a 15.00 MW Waste Heat Recovery System - progressed with the cement mill commissioned in July 2025 and the rest of the project to be commissioned in 2026-27; clinker for Line II grinding will be met from Line I clinkerisation. The Company has also identified opportunities to raise Kolimigundla cement grinding capacity from 1.50 MTPA to 3.00 MTPA, expected to be completed by March 2027, and management states Line II with 3.15 MTPA of clinker and 3 MTPA of cement is expected to be commissioned in March 2027. A Quartzite mineral has been included in the existing Andhra Pradesh mining lease, intended for manufactured sand and pozzolanic additives, with statutory approvals (mining plan, environmental clearance, consent to establish and operate) being pursued. De-bottlenecking continues as an economical route to capacity addition: at Ariyalur the Line I and Line II grinding systems have been de-bottlenecked, raising combined cement grinding capacity from 3.50 MTPA to 5.50 MTPA; at Ramasamy Raja Nagar ongoing work would raise clinkerisation from 2.14 MTPA to 2.76 MTPA and cement grinding from 3.00 MTPA to 4.00 MTPA; at Jayanthipuram clinker capacity would rise from 4.61 MTPA to 5.62 MTPA and cement capacity from 3.65 MTPA to 4.35 MTPA. For the proposed cement plant at Bommanahalli (Kalaburagi District, Karnataka) the Company became the Successful Bidder for the limestone block and had, as on 31st March 2026, acquired 966.725 acres of limestone bearing lands and 83.80 acres of factory land at a cost of Rs. 261.25 crores, with further acquisitions in progress; MoEF & CC has issued environmental clearance for mining of 4 MTPA of limestone, the Consent to Establish application is at final stages with KSPCB, and the time extension for execution of the mining lease deed is valid up to 10th May 2027, with Rs. 5.24 crores incurred on preliminary mining-related expenditure. In construction chemicals, the Company operates plants at Sriperumbudur, Salem, Ramasamy Raja Nagar and Jayanthipuram and commissioned its fifth plant at Haridaspur, Jajpur District, Odisha during the year. On green power, WHRS capacity was expanded from 45.15 MW to 53.15 MW. The Company states it incurred Rs. 996.65 crores towards capital expenditure during the year under review. Environmental impact assessments during the year covered the East Band Limestone Mine, Amalgamated Periyanagalur Limestone Mine, Ottakovil Limekankar Quarry Lease-2, Expansion of Kalavatla Line-II, Bommanalli Limestone Mine Block, Expansion of Ramasamy Raja Nagar Cement Plant, Maravarperungudi Lime Kankar Quarry Lease-III and Expansion of Jayanthipuram cement plant.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Extensive distribution ecosystem with 9,900+ dealers and 24,500+ sub-dealers
- Application-specific product architecture under the Right Product for the Right Application (RPRA) approach, spanning blended cement, OPC and construction chemicals
- Captive and green power integration - 53.15 MW WHRS, 165.79 MW wind farms and 193 MW thermal power - reducing dependence on purchased power
- Credit ratings of AA+ Stable (ICRA/CRISIL, long-term borrowings) and A1+ (short-term borrowings)
- Dedicated concrete testing laboratories across facilities and a MACE division that educates users on scientific application of products
- Regionally diversified integrated network across South and East India built from a single plant in Tamil Nadu, giving market proximity
- Adjacent construction chemicals platform (Hard Worker) extending the Company's role across the construction ecosystem, with 5.86 lakh tons sold in the year against 3.26 lakh tons in the previous year

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body: Fluctuations in raw material prices; Intense competition in the cement industry

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body: The company's credit rating is an important indicator of its financial health and ability to service its debt obligations.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Ramp up operations in 2026-27 by converting commissioned and to-be-commissioned capacity into productive volumes without compromising realisation quality
- Deepen channel presence by strengthening the next generation of dealer relationships in cement while scaling the Hard Worker construction chemicals distribution network across India
- Sustain financial momentum through margin recovery, cost management and further reduction of net debt as operating cash flows strengthen
- Prioritise margin recovery over volume-led growth in a soft pricing environment

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Regulation] Levy of mineral bearing land tax at Rs 160 per ton of limestone in Tamil Nadu, applicable from Apr-25, with an impact of ~Rs 39 crores for 1QFY27 (Rs 84 per ton of cement at company level) - a recurring structural cost, not a one-off.
- [FX / input risk] Deck attributes higher fuel cost to rupee depreciation, but states it two ways: "Rupee depreciation by 11% YoY during FY26" on the EBITDA slide and "rupee depreciation ~11% YoY during 1QFY27" on the power-and-fuel slide; INR is cited at record lows of ~96.5/USD.
- [Macro] Deck cites cement production up 9.8% YoY in Jun-26 (Index of Core Industries), Union budgeted capex of Rs 12.2 lakh crores for FY27, and Rs 5 Crores per region under City Economic Regions targeting Tier II/III cities and temple towns.
- [Brand] The "Hard Worker" campaign won six honours at the Kyoorius Creative Awards 2026 including the Grey Elephant Grand Prix for the Eco Plaster film, and seven awards at the Good Ads Matter Awards 2026.
- [Risk flagged by deck] "Sustainability of cement prices amid rising capacity additions / consolidation and competitive intensity", plus West Asia conflict / Strait of Hormuz pass-through into kiln fuel, freight, polymer and imported capex equipment costs.
